slides.title: Uric acid
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Blood or 24-hour urine

What it is used for: A blood test helps diagnose gout (usually together with synovial fluid analysis) and monitors uric acid during chemotherapy or other cancer treatment: when cancer cells are killed quickly they release large amounts of purines, and testing helps catch a rise early.
A urine test helps find out whether high uric acid is causing kidney stones and monitors the risk of kidney stones in people with gout.

Physiology: Uric acid is a normal waste product formed when the body breaks down purines, which are released from dying cells and found in certain foods and drinks. Normally it dissolves in blood, is filtered by the kidneys and leaves the body in urine.

slides.title: Uric acid
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: If the body makes too much uric acid or the kidneys remove too little, it builds up in blood and can form needle-shaped crystals in and around joints (gout). High levels can also cause kidney stones or kidney failure, but not everyone with high levels develops these problems.

slides.title: Uric acid
bullets: High: High blood uric acid may occur when the body makes too much or the kidneys cannot remove enough. Eating many purine-rich foods can also raise it: red and organ meats (liver, kidney), some seafood (shellfish, anchovies, sardines, trout, tuna), all types of alcohol and high-fructose corn syrup in soda and sweets.

High: Conditions that may be related to high blood uric acid include gout, kidney disease or kidney stones, leukemia, multiple myeloma, metastatic cancer, side effects of cancer treatment such as chemotherapy, alcohol use disorder and preeclampsia.

High: High urine uric acid may be related to gout, kidney stones or a high risk of them, leukemia, multiple myeloma or metastatic cancer, obesity, or an inherited genetic condition such as Lesch–Nyhan syndrome.

slides.title: Uric acid
bullets: Low: Low blood uric acid is uncommon and usually does not cause health problems; related conditions are usually diagnosed with other tests.
Low: Low urine uric acid may be related to kidney disease, lead poisoning or alcohol use disorder.

slides.title: Uric acid
bullets: Pre-analytics: The urine test requires collecting all urine for 24 hours: the first void is discarded and its time recorded, then all urine for the next 24 hours goes into the container. During collection the container is kept in a refrigerator or a cooler with ice.

Interferences: Many medicines, including aspirin, can affect uric acid levels in blood and urine, and taking niacin (vitamin B3) can also affect results. All medicines taken should therefore be reported.
Limitations: A high uric acid in blood or urine does not always mean a condition that needs treatment—many people have high levels without health problems. More tests may be needed to find the cause.

slides.title: Gout
bullets: Gout is typically diagnosed during a flare, when uric acid crystals in the joint are easiest to spot. Diagnosis uses a physical exam, x-rays, lab tests and history; not everyone with high uric acid develops gout.

Laboratory diagnosis of gout?
bullets: 1. Gout is the deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in joints and tissues; underlying it is prolonged hyperuricemia.

2. Definitive diagnosis: finding MSU crystals in synovial fluid or a tophus on polarized-light microscopy (needle-shaped crystals) – the "gold standard"; this is a sufficient criterion in the ACR/EULAR 2015 criteria.
3. Serum uric acid: supports the diagnosis but does not make it alone – it may be normal during an attack, and hyperuricemia occurs without gout; measured when not on urate-lowering therapy.
4. Synovial fluid analysis: leukocytes raised (inflammation), Gram stain and culture to exclude septic arthritis; differentiation from calcium pyrophosphate crystals (pseudogout).
5. Additional: creatinine/eGFR, urinary urate excretion and urinary stones, metabolic syndrome parameters (glucose, lipids).
